name: Local inference runtimes
summary: Programs such as llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio that run downloaded model files on your own computer instead of a remote service.

D1.guide: Look at the stack: which layer decides whether the model fits?
text: Some AI models can be downloaded as one big file, like a film you keep instead of stream.
A local runtime is the player for that file. It runs the model on your own computer, so your words never leave the house.
The catch: the file has to fit in your computer's memory.
D1.analogy: Downloading a film instead of streaming it.

text: A **local runtime** loads a model's weights into your GPU or CPU memory and generates tokens on your machine. Popular ones include llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio.

Models are usually shared as single files that bundle the weights, the tokenizer and settings such as the chat template. **GGUF** is a common format, and each model is often published in several quantization levels.
Most runtimes also start a small local server that speaks the same request format as the big cloud APIs, so existing apps and coding tools can point at your machine instead.
Memory decides what you can run: the weights (parameters × bits ÷ 8) plus the KV cache for your context must fit. Memory bandwidth then sets how fast tokens come out.

diagram.caption: What runs where when a model runs at home

D2.analogy: Downloading a film instead of streaming it.
D2.analogyBreaks: A downloaded film plays the same on any player. A model file can run noticeably differently depending on the quantization level, the runtime's settings and whether the chat template matches, and a big model may not fit at all.

predict.question: Your GPU has 24 GB of memory. Which model's weights fit with room left for the KV cache?
predict.explanation: Weights ≈ parameters × bits ÷ 8: 140, 35, 32 and 16 GB. Only the last fits in 24 GB with space left over for the KV cache.

text: The simple "does it fit" rule hides a lot. Splitting a model across several GPUs, or across GPU and system memory, works but slows generation, and machines with large shared memory change the trade-off between capacity and speed.

Quality at a given bit width varies by model and by quantization method, and community testing is often the only guide. Mismatched chat templates or tokenizer settings can quietly make a local model worse than the same model in the cloud.
